questions.why: Sex chromosomes behave as a pair in meiosis — they synapse and separate like homologs — although they differ in length and carry different genes. Only a small region of the Y matches the X.

questions.stem: A student editorial argues for a later start time but addresses "the school board" throughout, citing budget line items and district policy. Which revision best fits publication in the school newspaper?
options: Add more budget line items so the argument is fully documented.
Address the board more formally and use additional policy terminology.
Remove all evidence, since students do not care about facts.
Recast the claim around students' own experience and what they can ask the board to do.
questions.why: Audience determines which evidence and appeals are usable. Student readers need their own stake named and an action they can take, while budget detail aimed at the board reads as irrelevant to them.

questions.stem: Meiosis has one S phase but two divisions. What would follow if a cell replicated its chromosomes between meiosis I and meiosis II?
options: Each gamete would carry twice the DNA it should, undoing the reduction meiosis exists to produce.
Crossing over would occur a second time, doubling the variation.
Homologs would re-pair and rebuild the tetrads.
Nothing would change, because the second division would separate the extra copies.
questions.why: The point of two divisions after a single replication is to halve both chromosome number and DNA content. A second S phase would restore diploid DNA in every product.

questions.stem: A letter argues: "My opponent wants to cancel all sports so students can study more." The opponent's actual proposal adds one study hall each week. Which flaw is present?
options: Hasty generalization from a single example.
Circular reasoning that assumes the conclusion.
Straw man: the opponent's position is restated in an extreme form that is easier to attack.
Appeal to authority that substitutes prestige for evidence.
questions.why: The letter replaces the real proposal with a caricature — cancel all sports — and then refutes the caricature. That is a straw man, not an inference drawn from too little evidence.

questions.stem: A student writes: "Crossing over is how new alleles are created." Which correction is most accurate?
options: Crossing over creates new alleles whenever it occurs between non-sister chromatids.
Crossing over produces new combinations of alleles that already exist; only mutation creates new alleles.
Crossing over creates new alleles, but only during meiosis II.
Crossing over creates new alleles only in species that have many chromosomes.
questions.why: Recombination shuffles alleles that already exist, which is where most of a generation's variation comes from; the alleles themselves originate as mutations.

questions.stem: A board member defends a policy: "The new grading policy is fair, because it treats every student fairly." Which flaw is most precisely named?
options: False dilemma: only two options are considered.
Post hoc: sequence in time is treated as cause.
Ad hominem: critics are attacked instead of answered.
Circular reasoning: the conclusion is offered as its own justification.
questions.why: No independent reason is given — fair is simply asserted again in different words, so the sentence cannot support its own claim.

questions.stem: A plant cell is placed in a solution whose solute concentration is higher than the cell's. Which prediction about water movement and the cell's response is correct?
options: Water leaves the cell by osmosis, and the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall.
Water enters the cell, and turgor pressure rises.
Water moves equally in both directions, so the cell does not change.
Solutes move into the cell until concentrations match, so no water moves.
questions.why: Water moves toward the higher solute concentration, so a hypertonic bath pulls water out; in a plant cell the membrane then pulls away from the wall, which is plasmolysis.

questions.stem: An essay about a city's housing shortage ends: "So who exactly is the plan for?" What does closing on this question accomplish?
options: It restates the thesis in simpler language.
It introduces a new argument the essay never developed.
It leaves the reader to supply the damning answer the essay's evidence has made unavoidable.
It withdraws the essay's claim and leaves the issue open.
questions.why: The closing question delivers the essay's claim in the reader's own voice: the evidence has already pointed to an answer, and asking the question transfers the judgment to the reader.

questions.stem: A single nucleotide is deleted near the beginning of a coding sequence, and the resulting protein is nonfunctional. Which explanation best accounts for the effect?
options: The deletion removed the start codon, so translation never began at all.
The deletion shifted the reading frame, so every downstream codon was misread and the protein's sequence changed.
The deletion changed one codon, substituting a single amino acid for another.
The deletion added a stop codon at the same position, leaving the protein unchanged.
questions.why: A one-nucleotide deletion shifts the reading frame from that point onward, altering every downstream codon and usually producing an early stop — far more damaging than a single substitution.

questions.stem: A student measures reaction rate as substrate concentration rises. The rate climbs, then levels off, and adding more enzyme raises the plateau. Which best explains the plateau?
options: The reaction has reached equilibrium, so forward and reverse rates are equal and net product stops changing.
All active sites are saturated, so the rate is limited by the number of enzyme molecules rather than by substrate concentration.
The substrate has been entirely converted to product, so no further reaction can occur.
The enzyme denatures at high substrate concentration, permanently ending catalysis.
questions.why: The plateau is saturation: at high substrate concentration every active site is occupied, so the rate is capped by enzyme amount. That is why adding enzyme raises the plateau.

questions.stem: An editorial states: "Screens are almost certainly a factor in the decline, though the evidence so far is correlational, and the decline began before smartphones were widespread." The writer's qualifications chiefly serve to
options: build credibility by naming the limits of the evidence while still advancing the claim
concede that the claim is unsupported and should be withdrawn
shift blame from screens onto smartphones
signal that the writer has no position on the issue
questions.why: Naming the correlational limit and the timeline keeps the claim standing while showing the writer has weighed the evidence, which is what earns trust with a skeptical reader.

questions.stem: Isolated mitochondria are supplied with pyruvate and oxygen while a drug blocks the electron transport chain. Which immediate consequence best explains why ATP synthesis stops?
options: Pyruvate can no longer be oxidized to acetyl-CoA, so the citric acid cycle receives no carbon.
Cytosolic glycolysis halts because ATP synthase is the cell's only source of ATP.
Protons are no longer pumped into the intermembrane space, so the gradient driving ATP synthase collapses.
Oxygen binds ATP synthase directly and prevents phosphorylation of ADP.
questions.why: ATP synthase is a turbine run by the proton gradient. Blocking electron transport stops proton pumping, the gradient dissipates, and phosphorylation halts even though substrate is present.

questions.stem: A proposal opens with two captions: "The 1998 gym, before. The 2026 gym, after: same square footage, twice the students." It then argues for a new facility. The side-by-side captions chiefly
options: establish the writer's expertise in facilities planning
concede that the building has been well maintained
shift the argument from students to budgets
make the strain visible without the writer asserting it directly
questions.why: The juxtaposition lets the reader infer the crowding from the two facts, so the argument's premise arrives as an observation rather than as a claim the writer must defend.

questions.stem: A plant is given CO2 labeled with a heavy isotope under continuous light. In which molecule does the label first appear, and why?
options: In 3-phosphoglycerate, because rubisco fixes CO2 onto RuBP in the Calvin cycle.
In glucose, because the light reactions assemble sugar directly from CO2.
In oxygen, because CO2 is split at photosystem II.
In ATP, because the label enters the proton gradient before being fixed.
questions.why: Carbon fixation is the first step that incorporates CO2: rubisco attaches it to RuBP, and the unstable six-carbon product splits immediately into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate.

questions.stem: A student's essay opens by conceding that standardized tests predict first-year grades, then never mentions testing again while arguing for portfolio assessment. The chief problem with this concession is that it is
options: placed too early, which weakens the writer's ethos with a skeptical audience
dropped rather than answered, so it sits beside the argument instead of advancing it
insufficient, since one concession cannot satisfy opponents of the proposal
irrelevant, since first-year grades have nothing to do with assessment policy
questions.why: A concession earns its place only when the writer turns it — granting a point and then showing why the argument survives it. Left unanswered, it reads as an unrelated admission.

questions.stem: In a cell, DNA polymerase works normally but DNA ligase is nonfunctional. Replication opens the fork and then stalls on one new strand. Which best explains the stall?
options: Helicase cannot unwind the double helix without ligase, so the fork never opens.
Primase cannot lay down RNA primers, so synthesis never begins.
Topoisomerase cannot relieve supercoiling, so the fork reverses.
Okazaki fragments are synthesized but cannot be joined, leaving unsealed nicks in the lagging strand.
questions.why: Ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments. Without it the lagging strand accumulates unjoined fragments, while the continuously synthesized leading strand is largely unaffected.

questions.stem: An op-ed on school funding is written by a retired principal of thirty years in that district, and it opens: "I have sat in the meetings where these budgets were cut." The opening chiefly
options: establishes that the writer has read the budget documents
appeals to emotion by describing the length of the writer's career
grounds the writer's authority in direct experience of the specific decisions at issue
suggests that only career educators can evaluate a budget
questions.why: The claim to authority is narrow and specific — presence at those meetings — which is more persuasive than a general appeal to thirty years of service.

questions.stem: A mutation prevents the G1/S cyclin from being degraded. Which outcome is most likely, and why?
options: Cells pass the G1 checkpoint without the usual requirement for growth signals, favoring continued division.
Cells arrest in G2 permanently, because cyclin degradation is required for mitosis to begin.
Cells replicate their DNA twice per cycle, because S phase re-fires immediately after finishing.
Cells never enter mitosis, because cyclin must be destroyed to activate CDKs.
questions.why: Cyclin levels rise and fall to gate each transition; a cyclin that cannot be cleared keeps its CDK active, so the G1/S brake is released without the normal growth-signal requirement.

questions.stem: Defending a phone ban, a writer argues: "A hallway without a phone policy is a highway without lane markings — everyone is capable, and nobody is safe." The main weakness of the analogy is that it
options: compares places of very different size, so the comparison is factually inaccurate
relies on the audience's fear of accidents instead of evidence about learning
concedes that students are capable, which undercuts the case for a ban
assumes hallway order comes from a posted rule, which is the very point the argument needs to prove
questions.why: The analogy borrows the highway's case for markings and applies it to hallways, where order may come from supervision, schedules, or norms — so it assumes rather than supports the ban.

questions.stem: Researchers replace a membrane's unsaturated fatty acid tails with saturated ones and hold the temperature at 37 degrees C. What happens to fluidity, and why?
options: Fluidity rises, because saturated tails pack loosely and leave gaps.
Fluidity falls, because saturated tails pack more tightly and raise the temperature needed for the same fluidity.
Fluidity is unchanged, because cholesterol alone sets membrane fluidity.
Fluidity first rises and then falls, because saturated tails melt and then crystallize.
questions.why: Saturated tails lack the kinks that keep unsaturated tails apart, so they pack closely and stiffen the bilayer; the membrane needs a higher temperature to reach its previous fluidity.

questions.stem: An administrator's memo says a failing program will be "sunset" and that the affected families will be "transitioned to other options." The diction most likely
options: softens an ending by replacing plain terms with ones that sound procedural and inevitable
signals that the program's end is temporary and will be reviewed
shows that the administrator does not know which families are affected
appeals to families' emotions in order to win their support for the change
questions.why: "Sunset" and "transitioned" borrow the neutrality of a process, which removes the sense that anyone decided to end the program or that families are losing something.

questions.stem: A ligand binds a receptor tyrosine kinase whose kinase domain is inactive. Which step is blocked first, and why?
options: The ligand cannot bind the receptor, so no signal is received.
G proteins cannot exchange GDP for GTP at the receptor.
Receptor autophosphorylation fails, so adaptor proteins have no docking sites to recruit.
Second messengers cannot be degraded, so the signal never terminates.
questions.why: After dimerization the receptor phosphorylates itself, and those phosphotyrosines are what adaptor proteins bind. No kinase activity means no docking sites and no relay downstream.

questions.stem: After describing a flooded basement, mold in three classrooms, and a collapsed ceiling tile, a reporter writes: "The building has some maintenance needs." The understatement chiefly
options: shows that the reporter has not verified the extent of the damage
offers the district's perspective to balance the earlier details
signals that the damage is less serious than the paragraph suggested
lets the gap between the evidence and the wording carry the criticism
questions.why: The reader has just seen the list, so the mild phrasing lands as dry judgment: the writer never says the district is negligent, and does not have to.

questions.stem: An insect population is sprayed for ten generations. Resistance rises sharply and allele frequencies shift. Which statement best explains the shift?
options: The insecticide caused resistant mutations in individual insects, which then passed them to offspring.
Pre-existing resistant variants survived and reproduced more, so their alleles rose in frequency.
The insects learned to break down the insecticide and passed the learned trait to their offspring.
Gene flow from untreated populations introduced resistance alleles in every generation.
questions.why: Selection changes frequencies in a standing pool of variation; the mutations were already present at low frequency, and the spray removed the insects that lacked them.

questions.stem: A district newsletter praising its new "paperless initiative" arrives as a four-page color mailer to every household. The situation is ironic chiefly because
options: the format of the announcement contradicts the change it announces
the district spent money on printing during a budget crisis
households did not request the newsletter
the initiative is described as new when paperless systems are long established
questions.why: The irony is structural: the channel contradicts the message, since the claim to have gone paperless is printed on four pages of paper.

questions.stem: A cell has solute potential -0.6 MPa and pressure potential 0.2 MPa. It sits in a beaker whose solution has a water potential of -0.5 MPa. What is the direction of net water movement?
options: Out of the cell, because its solute potential is more negative than the solution's.
No net movement, because pressure potential cancels solute potential.
Into the cell, because the cell's water potential of -0.4 MPa is higher than the solution's -0.5 MPa.
Out of the cell, because pressure potential adds to the solute potential and lowers the total.
questions.why: Water potential is solute plus pressure: -0.6 + 0.2 = -0.4 MPa inside. Water moves from higher water potential (-0.4) toward lower (-0.5), so it enters the cell.

questions.stem: A student writes, "Reading scores fell six points (District Report 2025). This proves the curriculum failed," while the report itself attributes the fall to a new test format. The best revision is to
options: drop the citation, since the report contradicts the claim it is used to support
add a second citation that agrees with the claim so the evidence is balanced
keep the claim and note that the report's explanation is only one interpretation
report what the source actually says, including its explanation, and narrow the claim to what it supports
questions.why: Citing a source while suppressing its explanation misrepresents it. Honest integration states the finding and the caveat, then claims only what survives the caveat.

questions.stem: Two species share a trait their recent ancestors lacked, and the trait arises from different genes in each lineage. How should a phylogeneticist treat this trait?
options: As an analogous trait produced by convergent evolution, so it should not define a clade.
As a homologous trait inherited from a shared ancestor, so it does define a clade.
As a derived trait useful for rooting the tree at that node.
As an ancestral trait too widespread to be informative about relationships.
questions.why: Similar function built on different genes means independent origin. Grouping by that trait would create a false clade, which is why cladistics relies on shared derived homology.

questions.stem: A conclusion reads: "The district should fund tutors, extend library hours, and it should also be training teachers in reading instruction." The most useful revision chiefly
options: shortens the sentence so that each item receives equal emphasis
makes the three recommendations grammatically parallel so they read as one coordinated proposal
puts teacher training first, since it matters most
adds a fourth recommendation to show the scale of the problem
questions.why: The third item breaks the pattern with a new subject and verb, so it drops out of the list. Matching the form keeps all three inside a single, unified recommendation.

questions.stem: A storm reduces a fish population from 500 to 12 survivors. In the next generation an allele that had been rare is now common. Which best explains this?
options: Selection favored the allele during the storm, so the survivors were the fittest fish.
Mutation rates rose after the storm and produced the allele repeatedly.
The bottleneck sampled only a few alleles by chance, so drift shifted frequencies independently of fitness.
Gene flow from a larger population introduced the allele after the storm.
questions.why: A population crash leaves a random handful of alleles in the survivors. That is the bottleneck effect: frequency change from sampling, not from the allele being better suited to the habitat.

questions.stem: An essay argues schools should teach "media literacy" and spends its first body paragraph defining the term through three practices: tracing a claim to its source, following a statistic to its study, and reading a headline against its article. Defining the term this way chiefly
options: fixes a contested term to specific practices, so later claims can be evaluated
shows that media literacy is already taught in some schools
appeals to the audience's distrust of headlines
narrows the essay's audience to teachers who already agree
questions.why: A vague label invites agreement from everyone and commitment from no one. Defining it by practices converts it into something the argument can then show is missing or teachable.

questions.stem: In a bacterium, a repressor binds the operator only when a co-repressor is bound to it, and the structural genes are transcribed whenever the co-repressor is absent. What kind of control is this?
options: Positive control, because the co-repressor activates transcription of the operon
Inducible control, because transcription switches on when a substrate appears
Catabolite repression, because the available carbon source sets the transcription rate
Repressible negative control, because the repressor blocks transcription unless the co-repressor is absent
questions.why: The default state is on and the regulatory protein turns it off, so the control is negative; the product of the pathway activates the repressor, which is the signature of a repressible operon.

questions.stem: A college essay about a summer warehouse job is built from short declaratives and includes the line "I learned the difference between tired and unable." The style chiefly
options: demonstrates that the writer knows warehouse work from the inside
lets restraint carry the meaning, so the lesson arrives without being announced
shows that the writer is not yet ready for academic prose
creates suspense about whether the writer kept the job
questions.why: The clipped sentences withhold commentary, which makes the single reflective line do the work; the writer shows the lesson through pacing instead of stating it outright.

questions.stem: Fragments of 200, 800, and 2,000 base pairs are loaded into an agarose gel and electrophoresed. Which describes their final positions, and why?
options: The 2,000 bp fragment travels farthest, because it carries more net negative charge.
All three travel equally far, because their charge-to-mass ratios are equal and the gel cannot resolve size.
The 200 bp fragment travels farthest, because smaller fragments pass through the gel matrix more easily.
The 200 bp fragment travels least, because it binds more dye and becomes heavier.
questions.why: Agarose acts as a sieve: all fragments have nearly the same charge per unit mass, so the separating variable is length, and the shortest fragment moves fastest through the pores.

questions.stem: One paragraph ends "Costs rose 12 percent." The next begins "Meanwhile, enrollment fell." The transition is a poor choice chiefly because it
options: signals simultaneous time rather than the contrast or consequence the argument needs
is too informal for an academic essay
repeats the previous paragraph's point instead of advancing it
implies that the two trends cannot be compared
questions.why: "Meanwhile" marks two things happening at once. If the argument's point is that rising costs made falling enrollment worse, the transition hides the relationship the reader needs named.

questions.stem: After an infection a person carries antibody against the pathogen, and a second exposure triggers a faster, larger antibody response. Which cells account for this, and how?
options: Cytotoxic T cells, which retain antibody and release it on re-exposure
Helper T cells, which multiply and secrete antibody directly
Neutrophils, which remember the pathogen's surface and respond faster
Memory B cells, which survive and differentiate rapidly into antibody-secreting plasma cells
questions.why: The secondary response comes from long-lived memory B cells selected in the first infection: they are already present in higher numbers and need fewer signals to become plasma cells.

questions.stem: A column proposes that because students learn best when comfortable, schools should replace desks with beds and exams with naps. The proposal is satirical chiefly because it
options: cites no research on classroom furniture
extends a premise to an absurd conclusion in order to expose the premise's weakness
criticizes students for wanting to be comfortable
recommends a change the writer actually supports
questions.why: Satire follows a claim past the point where its advocates would go. The absurd extension makes the original premise look unexamined without the writer having to argue against it directly.

questions.stem: A tRNA's anticodon mutates so that it pairs with a stop codon, but the tRNA still carries its original amino acid. What is the most likely effect on translation?
options: Translation terminates earlier, because stop codons are recognized sooner.
The mRNA is degraded, because the ribosome detects the anticodon mismatch.
Translation reads past the normal stop and adds an amino acid, because the mutant tRNA competes with release factors.
The amino acid is left uncharged, so the protein comes out one residue shorter.
questions.why: A stop codon ends translation only because no tRNA answers it and a release factor binds instead. A tRNA that answers it inserts an amino acid, so the ribosome keeps going.

questions.stem: An argument states: "If we allow phones during passing periods, then we must allow them during class, and soon we will have no rules at all." The reasoning fails chiefly because it
options: treats a limited allowance as the first link in an inevitable chain without showing the chain is inevitable
compares passing periods with class time without explaining the comparison
offers no evidence about how phones affect learning
addresses an audience that does not actually set policy
questions.why: Each step is asserted, not argued: nothing shows that allowing phones in hallways requires allowing them in class. Without that link the conclusion does not follow from the premise.

questions.stem: A trophic pyramid shows 10,000 kcal at the producer level and about 1,000 kcal at the primary consumer level. Which best explains the loss?
options: Energy is destroyed as it moves up a trophic level, since consumers cannot use all of it.
Producers store only about 10 percent of the sunlight they absorb, so the rest never enters the food chain.
Primary consumers convert most ingested energy into new biomass, so the pyramid should widen upward.
Most energy leaves as heat from respiration and as undigested material, so roughly a tenth is built into consumer biomass.
questions.why: The ten percent rule reflects respiration losses and material that is not assimilated. Energy is not destroyed — it is converted to heat — so less remains to be passed on at each level.

questions.stem: A report finds that students who take four years of math are three times more likely to finish college. An editorial prints this as evidence that requiring four years of math will raise completion rates. The use is weakest because it
options: assumes the statistic is inaccurate without checking the study
converts a correlation among students who chose math into a claim about what a requirement would cause
fails to say which colleges the surveyed students attended
treats a threefold difference as too small to justify a policy
questions.why: Students who elect four years of math differ from those who do not in ways the statistic cannot separate. Turning that group difference into a predicted effect of a mandate is the leap.

questions.stem: On a hot, dry, windy afternoon a plant closes its stomata. Which immediate effect on water movement and photosynthesis is most likely?
options: Transpiration rises, because closing stomata concentrates water vapor inside the leaf.
Xylem tension falls and water uptake increases, because the pull from the leaves stops.
Transpiration falls and CO2 uptake drops, so the Calvin cycle slows for lack of carbon.
Root pressure alone maintains transpiration, so photosynthesis is unaffected.
questions.why: Stomata are both the exit for water vapor and the entrance for CO2. Closing them conserves water but starves the Calvin cycle of carbon, which is why photosynthesis drops at midday.
